displayQuote: A true friend is, as it were, a second self

meta.title: Who really said "A true friend is, as it were, a second self"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Cicero wrote it, in De Amicitia (44 BC), §80: a friend is “tamquam alter idem.” The idea itself goes back to Aristotle’s “another self.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A true friend is, as it were, a second self'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Cicero, from De Amicitia (44 BC), §80 — “tamquam alter idem.” The concept was first Aristotle’s “another self.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Cicero writes it in his dialogue Laelius de Amicitia (“On Friendship,” 44 BC), §80: a true friend is “tamquam alter idem” — “as it were, a second self.” The popular English is a faithful, lightly condensed rendering of that line (cf. E. S. Shuckburgh’s 1885 translation).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: §80 — “est enim is qui est tamquam alter idem”

source.excerpt: “For the man who keeps his eye on a true friend, keeps it, so to speak, on a model of himself. For this reason friends are together when they are separated, they are rich when they are poor, strong when they are weak, and — a thing even harder to explain — they live on after they have died… unless this feeling of love were reciprocated, a true friend would never be found; for a true friend is, as it were, a second self.”
trail: The Latin behind the line — “tamquam alter idem” — is confirmed in Cicero’s De Amicitia §80 on Perseus (Falconer, Loeb 1923) ↗.
The public-domain Shuckburgh (1885) translation ↗ renders the thought as a friend being “as it were a second self.”
The deeper root is Aristotle, who calls a friend “another self” (Ἑτερος αὐτός) in the Nicomachean Ethics, 1166a ↗.
source.excerptNote: Composite of Shuckburgh’s 1885 rendering around §80; Cicero’s Latin for the closing clause is “est enim is qui est tamquam alter idem.”

source.rightsNote: Cicero’s Latin (44 BC) is long in the public domain, and the standard English rendering by E. S. Shuckburgh dates to 1885 — well before 1931 — so the wording shown here carries no live copyright.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: Who was Cicero?
author.bio: Cicero was Rome’s greatest orator and a prolific philosopher who naturalized Greek thought in Latin. His late dialogue Laelius de Amicitia (44 BC) puts a meditation on friendship in the mouth of Gaius Laelius, and gave Latin the enduring formula for a friend as alter idem — “a second self.” Much of the West’s vocabulary for friendship descends from this text.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit?
misattribution.intro: The line is authentically Cicero’s, but its history has two honest complications worth flagging.

items.why: The concept of a friend as “another self” (Ἑτερος αὐτός) is Aristotle’s, stated in the Nicomachean Ethics, 1166a ↗, roughly three centuries before Cicero. Cicero gave it the Latin phrasing (alter idem) the English quote translates.

items.who: Cicero, but as a bare quote-card
items.why: Quote sites almost never cite the work: it is pinned to Cicero’s name with no locus (e.g. BrainyQuote ↗). The real home is De Amicitia §80, and the popular English is a condensed paraphrase rather than any one verbatim edition.

misattribution.truthLine: The verdict: genuinely Cicero, from De Amicitia §80 ↗ — a Latin echo of Aristotle’s older “another self.”

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Cicero’s De Amicitia was one of the most widely read texts of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, which is how “a second self” became the standard way to describe a true friend in European languages. The Latin alter idem and its cousin alter ego both flow from this tradition.
The paradox Cicero packs into two words — a friend who is at once other (alter) and identical (idem) — is exactly what has kept the line quotable for two millennia.
context.pull: A friend is “other” and “the same” at once — alter idem.
